system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Pathogenic NOTCH3 variants cause an autosomal dominant cerebral small-vessel arteriopathy. Mutant NOTCH3 extracellular-domain material accumulates around vascular smooth muscle cells, with progressive mural-cell degeneration and dysfunction that predispose to migraine, subcortical ischemic events, white-matter disease, and cognitive decline.
vignette: A 38-year-old woman is evaluated after a transient episode of left arm weakness. Since her 20s, she has had recurrent migraine with visual aura. Her father and paternal aunt both had strokes before age 55. Brain MRI shows multiple subcortical lacunar infarcts and symmetric white-matter hyperintensities involving the anterior temporal lobes and external capsules. She has no diabetes mellitus and has normal blood pressure.
lead: Which molecular mechanism most likely underlies this patient’s disorder?
correct: Aggregation of mutant NOTCH3 extracellular-domain protein around vascular smooth muscle cells, causing small-artery degeneration
distractors: Amyloid-beta deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessel walls, causing vessel-wall fragility
Defective type IV collagen in cerebral vascular basement membranes causing small-vessel fragility
Failure of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation causing energy-dependent stroke-like cortical lesions
Loss of ATP-dependent copper transport causing copper accumulation in the basal ganglia and liver
distractor_notes: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy involves amyloid-beta deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels and typically predisposes to lobar hemorrhage. It does not explain this autosomal dominant syndrome of migraine with aura, early subcortical infarcts, and characteristic anterior temporal/external-capsule white-matter lesions.
COL4A1-related small-vessel disease can cause hereditary cerebral arteriopathy and hemorrhage, but the classic CADASIL phenotype is caused by NOTCH3 pathology in vascular smooth muscle cells.

Mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS cause stroke-like episodes that typically do not respect vascular territories and are accompanied by systemic mitochondrial features; the family pattern is usually maternal rather than autosomal dominant.
ATP7B dysfunction causes Wilson disease with hepatic, psychiatric, and movement manifestations, not this inherited cerebral small-vessel pattern.
key_expl: The combination of migraine with aura, early recurrent subcortical ischemic events, autosomal dominant family history, and white-matter hyperintensities involving the anterior temporal poles and external capsules strongly suggests CADASIL. CADASIL is caused by pathogenic NOTCH3 variants. The abnormal NOTCH3 extracellular domain accumulates in and around the walls of small arteries near vascular smooth muscle cells, where it is associated with progressive smooth-muscle-cell degeneration and cerebral small-vessel dysfunction. Skin-biopsy electron microscopy can show characteristic granular osmiophilic material near vascular smooth muscle cells.
objective: Recognize CADASIL as an autosomal dominant NOTCH3-associated cerebral small-vessel arteriopathy characterized by migraine with aura, early subcortical strokes, characteristic white-matter lesions, and vascular smooth-muscle pathology.
clues: migraine with visual aura beginning in young adulthood
recurrent subcortical ischemic events at a young age
autosomal dominant family history of premature stroke
absence of major conventional vascular risk factors
